notes.summary: Mixture & Alligation covers combining two or more ingredients, solutions or groups and finding the resulting average, the mixing ratio, or the quantity to add, remove or replace. SSC CGL asks 1-2 questions per paper on price mixing, milk-water or acid concentration and repeated replacement, and the same alligation cross also solves average-marks, profit-percent, interest-rate and average-speed questions.
keyPoints: Alligation rule: Cheaper : Dearer = (Dearer − Mean) : (Mean − Cheaper). Example: ₹20 and ₹35 mixed to get ₹26 → (35 − 26) : (26 − 20) = 9 : 6 = 3 : 2.
Alligation works for any weighted average — prices, concentrations, average marks, profit %, interest rates, speeds — as long as you mix the quantities that carry the weights.
For average speed, the weights are TIMES, not distances, because average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
Three or more items: Mean = (q1 × p1 + q2 × p2 + q3 × p3) ÷ (q1 + q2 + q3).
Repeated replacement: removing x litres from V litres and refilling with water n times leaves V × (1 − x/V)ⁿ of the original liquid. Example: 40 L, remove 8 L twice → 40 × (4/5)² = 25.6 L.
Adding or evaporating water keeps the solute fixed: 30 kg of 10% salt solution has 3 kg salt; to make it 15%, the total must be 20 kg, so evaporate 10 kg of water.
Mixing two mixtures with different ratios: convert each to the fraction of one component (for example milk = 5/7 and 8/13), then apply alligation on those fractions.
Melting alloys of unequal weights: find the actual quantity of each metal in each alloy first, then add. Never add the ratio terms directly unless both ratios refer to equal weights.
Dishonest milkman: if water : milk = 1 : n and the mixture is sold at the cost price of milk, profit % = (1/n) × 100 (1 : 4 gives 25%).
traps: Reversing the alligation ratio: the difference on the dearer side gives the share of the CHEAPER item.
Using distance instead of time as the weight in average-speed alligation.
In replacement problems, forgetting that the removed portion also carries the solute (removing 20 L of a 40% solution removes 8 L of alcohol).
Adding ratio terms of two mixtures of different quantities (5:2 and 8:5 do not simply combine to 13:7).
Reporting the final total quantity when the question asks for the water added (or vice versa).
notes.examTip: Draw the alligation cross — two values on top, mean in the centre, differences diagonally — and most mixture questions finish in three lines without forming equations.

questions.text: In a class, the average marks of the boys are 70 and the average marks of the girls are 80. If the average marks of the whole class are 76, what is the ratio of the number of boys to the number of girls?
questions.explanation:
Apply alligation on the averages: boys 70, girls 80, mean 76.
Boys : girls = (80 − 76) : (76 − 70) = 4 : 6 = 2 : 3.
Check: (2 × 70 + 3 × 80) ÷ 5 = 380 ÷ 5 = 76.
Ratio = 2:3.

questions.text: Alloy A weighs 10 kg and contains copper and zinc in the ratio 3:2. Alloy B weighs 8 kg and contains copper and zinc in the ratio 1:3. If the two alloys are melted together, what is the ratio of copper to zinc in the new alloy?
questions.explanation:
Alloy A (10 kg, 3:2): copper = 6 kg, zinc = 4 kg.
Alloy B (8 kg, 1:3): copper = 2 kg, zinc = 6 kg.
Together: copper = 8 kg, zinc = 10 kg.
Ratio = 8 : 10 = 4 : 5. (17:23 would be correct only if equal weights were mixed.)

questions.text: How many litres of a 30% acid solution must be added to 20 litres of a 60% acid solution to obtain a 50% acid solution?
questions.explanation:
Alligation on concentrations 30% and 60% with mean 50%.
30% solution : 60% solution = (60 − 50) : (50 − 30) = 10 : 20 = 1 : 2.
The 60% solution is 20 L, so the 30% solution needed = 20 × 1/2 = 10 L.
Check: acid = 3 + 12 = 15 L in 30 L = 50%.

questions.text: Two varieties of tea costing ₹126 per kg and ₹135 per kg are mixed with a third variety in the ratio 1:1:2. If the mixture is worth ₹153 per kg, what is the price of the third variety per kg?
questions.explanation:
Let the third variety cost ₹x per kg.
Weighted average: (1 × 126 + 1 × 135 + 2 × x) ÷ 4 = 153.
So 261 + 2x = 612 → 2x = 351 → x = 175.50.
Price of the third variety = ₹175.50 per kg.

questions.text: A trader sold 50 kg of rice, part of it at 10% profit and the rest at 5% loss. If his overall profit was 4%, how many kg did he sell at 10% profit?
questions.explanation:
Treat the loss as −5% and apply alligation with mean 4%.
Part at 10% : part at −5% = (4 − (−5)) : (10 − 4) = 9 : 6 = 3 : 2.
Quantity sold at 10% profit = 3/5 × 50 = 30 kg.
Check: 30 × 10% − 20 × 5% = 3 − 1 = 2, which is 4% of 50.

questions.text: A sum of ₹5,000 is lent in two parts, one at 6% and the other at 10% per annum simple interest. If the total interest received after one year is ₹380, how much was lent at 6%?
A man covers 100 km in 10 hours, partly on foot at 4 km/h and partly by bicycle at 16 km/h. What distance did he cover on foot?
questions.explanation:
Average speed = 100 ÷ 10 = 10 km/h.
For speeds, alligation gives the ratio of TIMES: foot : cycle = (16 − 10) : (10 − 4) = 6 : 6 = 1 : 1.
So he walked for 5 hours and cycled for 5 hours.
Distance on foot = 5 × 4 = 20 km (cycle 80 km, total 100 km).

questions.text: A vessel contains 80 litres of a solution that is 40% alcohol. 20 litres of the solution are removed and replaced with pure alcohol. What is the percentage of alcohol in the new solution?
questions.explanation:
Alcohol initially = 40% of 80 = 32 L.
Removing 20 L of solution removes 40% of 20 = 8 L of alcohol, leaving 24 L of alcohol in 60 L.
Adding 20 L of pure alcohol: alcohol = 44 L in 80 L.
Percentage = 44 ÷ 80 × 100 = 55%.

questions.text: 40 kg of sea water contains 5% salt by weight. How much fresh water must be added so that the salt content becomes 2%?
questions.explanation:
Salt = 5% of 40 = 2 kg, and this amount does not change.
For salt to be 2% of the total, total weight = 2 ÷ 0.02 = 100 kg.
Fresh water to be added = 100 − 40 = 60 kg.

questions.text: A vessel contains 64 litres of pure milk. A certain quantity is taken out and replaced with water, and the process is repeated once more with the same quantity. If milk and water are now in the ratio 9:7, how many litres were taken out each time?
questions.explanation:
After two replacements of x litres, milk left = 64 × (1 − x/64)².
Milk is now 9/16 of the mixture, so (1 − x/64)² = 9/16 → 1 − x/64 = 3/4 → x = 16.
Check: milk 64 → 48 → 36 L, water = 28 L, and 36 : 28 = 9 : 7.
Quantity taken out each time = 16 L.

questions.text: Vessel A contains milk and water in the ratio 5:2, and vessel B contains milk and water in the ratio 8:5. In what ratio should the contents of A and B be mixed to get a mixture with milk and water in the ratio 9:4?
questions.explanation:
Milk fraction in A = 5/7, in B = 8/13, required = 9/13.
Alligation: A : B = (9/13 − 8/13) : (5/7 − 9/13) = 1/13 : 2/91.
Multiply both by 91: A : B = 7 : 2.
Check: 7 L of A + 2 L of B gives milk 5 + 16/13 = 81/13 and water 2 + 10/13 = 36/13, i.e. 81 : 36 = 9 : 4.
Required ratio = 7:2.
